title: 1.5.45 Module 1.5 Quiz
description: Twelve multiple-choice questions on computational thinking, decomposition, abstraction, pseudocode, flowcharts, recursion and debugging. Checked instantly.

questions.question: Which is the best description of computational thinking?
options: Learning to think the way a computer does
Memorising the syntax of a programming language
A way of tackling a problem: break it down, spot what repeats, ignore what does not matter, and lay out precise steps
Doing arithmetic quickly in your head
questions.explanation: It is a way of approaching a problem, and it has nothing to do with thinking like a machine — people used it long before computers existed.

questions.question: What are the four techniques of computational thinking?
options: Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking
Design, development, testing and deployment
Sequence, selection, repetition and recursion
Reading, writing, running and debugging
questions.explanation: Those four. The second list is the software life-cycle, and the third is structured programming — different ideas that are easy to mix up.

questions.question: Why is working out a plan before typing usually faster than typing your way to an answer?
options: Typing slowly is bad for your hands
You separate deciding what to do from getting it past the computer, so you only fight one problem at a time
Planning is required before the browser will run your code
It is not faster — it just looks more professional
questions.explanation: Typing your way to an answer means solving the problem and satisfying the syntax at the same time. Planning first splits those apart, and a wrong plan is far cheaper to throw away than wrong code.

questions.question: In a flowchart, what do the oval, the rectangle and the diamond mean?
options: Oval = a decision, rectangle = start or end, diamond = a step
Oval = start or end, rectangle = a step, diamond = a decision
Oval = a step, rectangle = a decision, diamond = start or end
Oval = input, rectangle = output, diamond = a step
questions.explanation: Table 1.5.2: oval for start and end, rectangle for a step, diamond for a decision. (This course adds a parallelogram for input and output — see 1.5.29.)

questions.question: Which flowchart shape has two arrows leaving it, and why?
options: The oval, because a program can start in two places
The rectangle, because a step can succeed or fail
The diamond, because it asks a question and the answer sends you down the yes path or the no path
All of them have two arrows leaving
questions.explanation: The diamond is the only one that branches. Everything else has exactly one way out — which is what keeps a chart readable.

questions.question: Which statement is true about pseudocode and flowcharts?
options: Pseudocode is faster to write and edit; a flowchart makes branching obvious at a glance
A flowchart is faster to write; pseudocode is better for showing branches
Pseudocode is better in every way, which is why flowcharts are no longer used
They are the same thing — one is just drawn instead of typed
questions.explanation: They fail in opposite directions. Pseudocode stays a list and scales to long programs; a flowchart gets enormous, but you can see a branch instead of tracing it.

questions.question: What is a base case, and what happens without one?
options: The first line of any program — without one the program will not start
The stopping condition in a recursive function — without one it calls itself forever and crashes
The simplest test case you write — without one you cannot check your work
The default branch of an if statement — without one nothing happens
questions.explanation: The base case is the case that does not recurse. Leave it out and the function keeps calling itself until the browser gives up with a stack overflow.

questions.question: An error message has three useful parts. Which are they?
options: The file, the author and the date
The warning, the suggestion and the fix
The kind of error, the detail about what went wrong, and the place it happened
The line number, the column number and the character
questions.explanation: In `Uncaught ReferenceError: totl is not defined at line 3` — the kind is ReferenceError, the detail names your typo exactly, and the place is line 3.

questions.question: Why is `console.log("total is " + total)` more useful than `console.log(total)`?
options: It runs faster
It prints the value more accurately
When several values print, the label tells you which number you are looking at
Without the label the value will not print at all
questions.explanation: A column of bare numbers tells you nothing about which is which. Labelling each one is the difference between output you can debug with and output you have to guess at.

questions.question: You have broken a problem into parts. What tells you a part is genuinely self-contained?
options: You could hand it to someone else with no further explanation and get it back working
It fits on one line
It takes less than five minutes
It comes first in the list
questions.explanation: A part you can only understand while holding three others in your head has been chopped, not decomposed.

questions.question: Deciding whether to keep a detail, what is the test?
options: Does dropping it change what the reader has to do?
Is it true?
Is it interesting?
Does it make the description shorter?
questions.explanation: Being true is not the standard. A detail can be perfectly true and still worth discarding.

questions.question: In pseudocode, what is indentation doing?
options: Showing which steps are inside which
Making the plan look tidy
Marking the most important lines
Standing in for semicolons
questions.explanation: Move one line in or out by four spaces and you have described a different program.
